Issued at 205 PM CST Sun Nov 15 2026

A shortwave passing through the northern Plains this afternoon 
is displacing an omega block to the east of the forecast area, 
promoting a southwesterly flow patter that will persist through 
the early portions of this coming workweek. Mild, dry, and calm 
weather can mainly be anticipated during this period, though 
breezy south to southeast winds, sustained around 15 MPH and 
gusting as high as 25 MPH, will be possible in the southern 
James River Valley as a mild MSLP gradient lingers over eastern 
North Dakota. Patchy fog will be possible over portions of 
southwestern into south central North Dakota tonight into Monday
morning as a very shallow saturated layer develops and as winds
become very light overnight, though confidence in significant 
visibility reductions is low at this time. Otherwise, mild 
temperatures with highs in the 50s and lows in the 30s are 
expected through Tuesday night. 

Early Wednesday into Thursday, a robust shortwave impulse 
ejecting out of the Pacific Northwest is progged to cross the 
Rockies, with with lee cyclogenesis spitting a surface low 
pressure system over central Montana. The passage of this low 
pressure system across North Dakota is expected to promote low 
to medium chances across much of the forecast area. The ensemble
is beginning to favor a more northerly track for this system, 
pushing the axis of highest QPF (approaching 0.25") further 
northwest North Dakota and Canada. Light QPF (around 0.10") can 
still be anticipated elsewhere, though portions of the far south
central into southeastern North Dakota may fall under the dry 
slot. While mainly rain is anticipated with this system, a 
transition to some snowfall is possible across the northwest 
into the north central during the coolest portions Wednesday 
night into Thursday morning. Little to no accumulating snowfall 
is generally not anticipated, though a minority cluster (approx.
30 percent of ensemble members, mainly from the GEPS with some 
ENS) does advertise a dusting of snow across the far northwest 
by Thursday morning. This system also represents a downward turn
for temperatures across western and central North Dakota, with 
highs dropping back down into the 30s west to 40s east for 
Wednesday and Thursday. Gusty west to northwest, sustained 
around 25 to 30 MPH and gusting as high as 40 MPH, can also be 
anticipated the surface pressure gradient tightens across the 
southwest. 

Chances for precpitation will again increase across the area 
through the day Friday a strong Pacific Northwestern low crosses
over the Rockies and slides across the northern Plains. The 
passage of this system will again spit out a lee side low, this 
time over Wyoming, and loft it across the northern Plains, 
promoting chances for precipitation across portions of North 
Dakota. The ensemble has developed decent agreement on the storm
track, with the low passing across South Dakota into Minnesota,
though differences in relative strength of the system and it's 
timing persist. Cluster analysis reveals two potential 
scenarios. The less impactful of the two, where a faster moving 
open wave passes through the region, is slightly favored at this
time (60 percent of ensemble members). With less residence 
time, and with a late transition from rain to snow Saturday 
morning, overall snowfall would be somewhat light for most 
portions of the forecast area, around 1 inch or so. Portions of 
the northwest and north could approach 2 inches depending on how
much wrap- around precpitation lingers through the day on 
Saturday, but the chances for this are low in this scenario. A 
slower moving, stacked system is also possible (40 percent of 
ensemble members), and would be the more impactful of the two. 
Greater residence time precipitation, and a greater amount of 
precpitation would fall as accumulating snowfall. In this 
scenario, much of the west and north central has a medium chance
to exceed 2 inches of snowfall, and a low chance to approach 4 
inches overall in the northwest. Scenario 1 is fairly well 
dispersed between all parent model families, but scenario 2 is 
underdispersed and is highly influenced by the most aggressive 
members of the GEPS. In either scenario, cooler temperatures 
with highs mainly in the 30s can be anticipated through the 
weekend into early next week on the backside of this system.
